interactions.label: Why is the first-trimester ultrasound scan between 11 and 14 weeks considered th

params.question: Why is the first-trimester ultrasound scan between 11 and 14 weeks considered the single most important investigation in a newly diagnosed twin pregnancy?

answers.text: It detects congenital anomalies more accurately than a second-trimester scan

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The detailed anomaly scan is performed at 18 to 20 weeks, not in the first trimester. The first-trimester scan's primary value lies in determining chorionicity, not anomaly detection.

answers.text: It determines chorionicity with over 95% accuracy, which governs the entire surveillance and delivery plan

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Chorionicity is the single most important prognostic factor in twin pregnancy, and it can only be reliably determined in this narrow window before the inter-twin membrane thickens.

answers.text: It can predict whether twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome will develop later in pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TTTS cannot be predicted at this stage. However, identifying monochorionic placentation at this scan alerts clinicians to begin the closer surveillance that can detect TTTS when it develops.

answers.text: It accurately estimates individual fetal weights to detect early growth restriction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fetal weight estimation becomes relevant from the mid-second trimester onward. The first-trimester scan's unique and irreplaceable value is in determining chorionicity.

overallFeedback.feedback: The first-trimester USS uniquely determines chorionicity with over 95% accuracy. After 14 weeks, membrane thickening makes this assessment unreliable, yet chorionicity governs every subsequent management decision.
Exactly right. After 14 weeks the inter-twin membrane thickens, making chorionicity much harder to determine — so this first-trimester window is irreplaceable for planning the entire pregnancy.

interactions.label: On first-trimester ultrasound, an inter-twin membrane meets the placenta at a sh

params.question: On first-trimester ultrasound, an inter-twin membrane meets the placenta at a sharp right angle, forming a T-shape. What does this finding indicate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dichorionic twins show a lambda (twin peak) sign, where a wedge of placental tissue from both placentas pushes into the membrane base — not a sharp right-angle T-shape.
Correct. In monochorionic twins the inter-twin membrane is composed only of amnion, with no intervening chorionic tissue, so it meets the single shared placenta at a sharp right angle — the T-sign.

answers.text: Monochorionic monoamniotic twins sharing one amniotic sac

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Monoamniotic twins have no inter-twin membrane at all. If a membrane is visible forming a T-sign, the twins must have separate amniotic sacs — making them monochorionic diamniotic.

answers.text: A normal singleton pregnancy with a uterine septum mimicking a membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A uterine septum does not produce an inter-twin membrane with a T-sign. This sign is specific to monochorionic twin pregnancies where only amniotic layers form the dividing membrane.

overallFeedback.feedback: The T-sign indicates monochorionic diamniotic twins. Unlike the lambda sign (where villi from two placentas push into the membrane base), the T-sign shows only amniotic membrane meeting a single shared placenta at a right angle.
Well done. The T-sign confirms a shared placenta, which means these twins need closer surveillance — fortnightly scans from 16 weeks — because of the risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

interactions.label: Monochorionic diamniotic twins should be delivered at 38 weeks, the same gestati

params.question: Monochorionic diamniotic twins should be delivered at 38 weeks, the same gestational age as dichorionic diamniotic twins.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. Because monochorionic diamniotic twins share a single placenta, they face risks like twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and require earlier delivery at 36 to 37 weeks. The 38-week target applies only to dichorionic diamniotic twins, the lower-risk category.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Monochorionic diamniotic twins share one placenta that ages faster and carries the risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, so they are delivered earlier at 36 to 37 weeks. Only dichorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at 38 weeks.

interactions.label: In twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, blood flows unevenly between twins through

params.question: In twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, blood flows unevenly between twins through shared placental vessels. Which of the following best describes the resulting pathological consequence for the affected twins?

answers.text: Both twins develop polyhydramnios from increased circulating volume

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Only the recipient twin develops polyhydramnios from volume overload. The donor twin, losing blood through the shared vessels, becomes fluid-depleted — this asymmetry is the hallmark of TTTS.

answers.text: One twin becomes fluid-depleted while the other becomes fluid-overloaded

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The unbalanced blood flow through shared placental anastomoses causes the donor to become fluid-depleted and the recipient to become volume-overloaded, creating the characteristic amniotic fluid discordance that clinicians watch for.

answers.text: Both twins develop symmetrical growth restriction from overall placental insufficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: TTTS is not about overall placental insufficiency — it is specifically about unequal distribution of blood flow between the twins. The consequences are asymmetric, not symmetrical.

answers.text: The donor twin develops polycythaemia while the recipient twin becomes anaemic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes twin anaemia-polycythaemia sequence (TAPS), a different condition involving slow haemoglobin transfer. In TTTS, the primary pathology is volume imbalance causing amniotic fluid discordance, not primarily a haemoglobin difference.

overallFeedback.feedback: In TTTS, blood flows unevenly through shared placental vessels: one twin loses volume (becomes fluid-depleted) while the other gains excess volume (becomes fluid-overloaded). This asymmetric fluid discordance is the hallmark finding that fortnightly scans are designed to detect.

Exactly. This fluid discordance is why monochorionic twins need fortnightly scanning from 16 weeks. Left untreated, TTTS carries an extremely high risk of fetal death, which is why staging systems and fetoscopic laser ablation exist.
